parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: The cell has negligible internal resistance, so think about how much of the 1.3 V e.m.f. appears as potential difference across wire X of resistance 1.1 ohm, and how potential difference and resistance determine current.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link e.m.f. to p.d. across X**
You are sitting with a single loop circuit. Because the cell has negligible internal resistance there is no lost volts inside the cell, so the full e.m.f. of $1.3\text{ V}$ appears across the external wire X.

Step 2: **Apply resistance to find current**
For a metallic wire, $$I = \frac{V}{R}$$ So $$I = \frac{1.3}{1.1} = 1.18 \approx 1.2\text{ A}$$ This is the current in X and also the ammeter reading.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Current is the flow of many electrons drifting slowly. Think about what controls how fast they must drift: the current you just found, how many electrons per cubic metre are available, their charge, and the area they squeeze through.
Hint 2: Use $I = nqvA$ rearranged for $v$, with $q = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, $n = 8.5 \times 10^{28}\text{ m}^{-3}$ and $A = 4.7 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}^2$. Check powers of ten carefully.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Picture drift speed**
Current does not mean electrons race round at high speed. They have random thermal motion plus a tiny average drift along the wire. More current, or fewer carriers, or a smaller area means they must drift faster. This is summarised by $$I = nqvA$$ where $n$ is number density, $q$ is electron charge and $A$ is cross-sectional area.

Step 2: **Rearrange and substitute**
You need $v$: $$v = \frac{I}{nqA}$$ Using $I = 1.2\text{ A}$ from (a)(i): $$v = \frac{1.2}{(8.5 \times 10^{28})(1.60 \times 10^{-19})(4.7 \times 10^{-7})}$$ The denominator is $6.39 \times 10^{3}$, so $$v = 1.9 \times 10^{-4}\text{ m s}^{-1}$$ This tiny value, less than a millimetre per second, is typical for drift speed.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
hints: Hint 1: Resistance depends on size, but resistivity is the material property behind it. Think about how length makes resistance larger and area makes it smaller, and which quantities you know for wire X.
Hint 2: Recall the relation linking $R$, $\rho$, $L$ and $A$, and first convert the length from 45 cm to metres in SI units.
Hint 3: Substitute $R = 1.1\text{ }\Omega$, $A = 4.7 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}^2$ and $L = 0.45\text{ m}$ to evaluate $\rho$ in $\Omega\text{ m}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Separate material from shape**
Resistance $R$ changes if you cut the wire. Resistivity $\rho$ does not - it describes nichrome itself. A longer wire gives electrons more to push through, a wider wire gives more parallel paths, so $$R = \frac{\rho L}{A}$$

Step 2: **Rearrange for resistivity**
You know $R$, $L$ and $A$, so $$\rho = \frac{RA}{L}$$ Remember to use metres: $45\text{ cm} = 0.45\text{ m}$.

Step 3: **Calculate**
$$\rho = \frac{1.1 \times 4.7 \times 10^{-7}}{0.45}$$ $$\rho = 1.1 \times 10^{-6}\text{ }\Omega\text{ m}$$ to 2 significant figures. This large value compared to copper is why nichrome is used for heating elements.

parts.label: (b)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Adding Y in parallel gives the current a second identical path. Think about what happens to the combined resistance of X and Y compared to X alone.
Hint 2: The cell e.m.f. is unchanged, so think about how total current from the cell, measured by the ammeter, responds when total resistance falls with the same p.d.
parts.proper_answer: Total resistance decreases to half, p.d. stays at 1.3 V, so total current and ammeter reading increase (doubles to about 2.4 A).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See the effect on total resistance**
X and Y are identical resistors in parallel. Two equal paths conduct better than one, so combined resistance is $R/2 = 0.55\text{ }\Omega$. In general adding a parallel branch always lowers total resistance.

Step 2: **See the effect on total current**
The cell still provides $1.3\text{ V}$ with negligible internal resistance, so p.d. across the combination is still $1.3\text{ V}$. With $$I_{total} = \frac{V}{R_{total}}$$ a smaller $R_{total}$ with the same $V$ gives a larger $I_{total}$. The ammeter is in the main line and reads this total current, so its reading increases.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
key_concepts: drift speed depends on branch current
hints: Hint 1: Drift speed in X depends only on the current in X itself. Think about whether the p.d. across X, and hence its own branch current, has changed when Y was added in parallel.
parts.proper_answer: No change - the p.d. across X and the current in X are unchanged, so $v = I/nqA$ for X is the same.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Focus on branch X alone**
In parallel both X and Y still have the full $1.3\text{ V}$ across them. So the current through X stays at $1.2\text{ A}$ as in (a)(i); the extra total current goes through Y. Since $v = I/nqA$ and $I$, $n$, $q$, $A$ for X are all unchanged, the average drift speed in X stays the same. A common mistake is to use the larger total current for X.
